events.name: type_level_reference
events.reason: fitting failed: type_level_reference: the fit did not finish within 30 minutes
events.hypothesis: People interpret and produce referring expressions by reasoning over perceptual equivalence classes (referential types) rather than raw object tokens: identical visual objects in a scene are perceptually grouped into a single type, and communicative speakers choose utterances to distinguish the target's type from alternative types. events.name: contrast_deficit_speaker
events.reason: fitting failed: contrast_deficit_speaker: the fit did not finish within 30 minutes

On informative trials, this parsimony penalty prevents visual singleton salience from spuriously overriding communicative informativeness for multi-feature competitors, while on uninformative displays visual attention defaults to contextually unique singletons. Differences from bounded_depth_listener: recursion depth remains depth 1 (listener calls L1); parameter beta is added with prior dist.LogNormal(0.0, 1.0); no parameters are removed (retaining alpha and w_singleton); L1 adds feature_count to its signature and scales referent choice weights by exp(-beta * vec(feature_count, r)); and listener passes beta and ctx.feature_count into L1 on informative trials.

live.name: feature_uncertainty_listener_2
live.hypothesis: Listeners interpret referring expressions under referential feature uncertainty, being unsure which visual feature of a candidate referent the speaker intended to pick out. When evaluating literal semantics, listeners weight an object's compatibility by the probability that the speaker chose the heard feature from that object's feature bundle, naturally favoring minimal referents whose features are exhaustively described over cluttered multi-feature competitors. Communicative speakers select expressions expecting this feature-attribution inference, while spontaneous visual attention on uninformative displays defaults to contextually unique singletons.
